Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Failing scenario in the test suite:
  - The last assertion in testMultiply checks that field.newDfp("1").multiply(10000) equals field.newDfp("10000") (lines 909–911, “Multiply #37”).
  - Expected: 1 × 10000 = 10000.
  - Actual behavior: the operation returns NaN and sets the invalid flag, causing the test to fail.

- Code path taken:
  - org.apache.commons.math3.dfp.Dfp.multiply(int) simply delegates to multiplyFast(x) (lines 1602–1604).
  - In multiplyFast(int x), there is an explicit range check (lines 1634–1641):
    - If x < 0 or x >= RADIX, the method sets the IEEE invalid flag, constructs a zero, marks it as a quiet NaN (QNAN), and returns that result.
    - Dfp.RADIX is 10000.
  - Since the test calls multiply(10000), x == RADIX triggers this path and returns NaN rather than performing the intended multiplication.

- Why this violates the contract and test expectations:
  - The interface org.apache.commons.math3.FieldElement.multiply(int) declares multiplication by any integer n (“n × this” with no restriction on n).
  - Dfp.multiply(int) is improperly constrained to 0 <= x < RADIX, rejecting x == RADIX and any larger magnitude (and even negative values), which contradicts the general contract and typical mathematical expectation.
  - For the particular failing test, multiply(10000) should be valid: 1 × 10000 = 10000. The current implementation’s fast path limitation produces NaN instead, hence the failure.

- Additional observations:
  - Dfp.multiply(Dfp) (lines 1496–1596) correctly handles general multiplication with no such restriction and would handle 10000 if passed as a Dfp (e.g., newDfp(10000) or from string).
  - The special-case handling in multiplyFast (lines 1614–1632) correctly manages NaN and infinities for small x, but the range check (x < 0 || x >= RADIX) short-circuits legitimate integer multiplications far beyond the base digit range.
  - Therefore, the root cause is the unconditional delegation of multiply(int) to multiplyFast(int) combined with multiplyFast’s restrictive range check, causing valid integer multiplications (like 10000) to be treated as invalid.

In summary, Dfp.multiply(int) violates FieldElement.multiply(int) by rejecting integers outside [0, RADIX-1]. This manifests in testMultiply “#37” where multiply(10000) returns NaN due to the range check in multiplyFast, instead of producing 10000. The remedy is to make multiply(int) support all int values, keeping the fast path only for |x| < RADIX and falling back to the general Dfp×Dfp path (or equivalent decomposition) otherwise.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
